column4: The two sons of Adam are introduced as brothers, and one explicitly threatens to kill the other; this establishes the family relation and threatened bloodshed completed in 5:30.
The servants of the Merciful neither kill a soul God has made inviolable except by right nor commit other grave crimes; the ayah states the homicide boundary before its divine penalty.
The murderer's punishment is multiplied and made abiding and humiliating, shifting the blood crime of 25:68 into a requital beyond a human guardian's power.
Repentance, faith, and good work can transform evil deeds into good, a merciful reversal to 25:69's otherwise multiplied requital.
Noah's people are drowned, made a sign for humanity, and assigned a prepared punishment, explicitly joining exemplary destruction to recompense held ready.
ʿĀd and Thamud are inserted into the same catalogue of destroyed peoples, repeating two of the section's named examples.
Examples were set forth to each listed people and each was utterly destroyed, stating why the catalogue in 25:37–38 functions as warning.
Noah's people, ʿĀd, and Thamud are grouped as prior deniers, beginning a warning list whose delayed seizure is stated in 22:44.
After adding Moses to the rejected messengers, God says He granted the deniers respite and then seized them, a precise sequence of watchful delay and requital.
Noah's people, the people of the well, and Thamud begin another catalogue of communities that denied before the present hearers.
ʿĀd and Pharaoh are added to the catalogue containing Thamud, again gathering the section's exemplary peoples.
Every listed people denied the messengers, so God's threatened punishment became due; the verdict makes 50:12–13's names punitive examples.
ʿĀd denies, and the surrounding refrain asks the reader to consider God's punishment and warnings, explicitly presenting the people as a deterrent case.
After ʿĀd's destruction, the refrain again asks how God's punishment and warnings were, fixing the episode's exemplary function.
Thamud denies the warnings, beginning a parallel exemplary cycle immediately after the ʿĀd cycle.
The Thamud cycle ends with the same question about God's punishment and warnings, marking its destruction as another deterrent example.
Warnings reach Pharaoh's people, introducing the third of the section's named civilizations into the repeated pattern.
Pharaoh's people deny all the signs and are seized by One mighty and fully able, supplying the unmatched requital that completes 54:41.
The audience is warned of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of ʿĀd and Thamud, directly turning their punishments into a threatened precedent.
Every soul will be paid in full for what it earned and none will be wronged, an exact formulation of recompense preserved until the return to God.
On the indisputable Day, every soul is paid in full for what it earned without injustice; no blood claim or deed disappears before account.
God does not wrong even an atom's weight and multiplies a good deed, sharpening both exact liability and generous repayment.
The Lord will pay every person fully for their deeds because He knows what they do, directly restating the section's kept recompense.
God does not let the reward of those who do good be lost, another exact formulation of beneficence held until repayment.
Each soul comes pleading for itself and is paid fully for what it did without injustice, placing exact repayment in the final court.
No soul is wronged at all on that day and people are repaid only for what they did, a concise account of measured divine requital.
Every soul is paid fully for what it did after the record and witnesses are brought, so the final judgment leaves no claim unpaid.
Creation in truth serves a judgment in which each soul is repaid for what it earned and none is wronged, matching the section's assured counterpayment.
Every person has degrees according to deeds so God may pay them fully, with no injustice; earned differences are preserved until recompense.
God owns all that is in heaven and earth so He may repay evildoers for their deeds and reward good-doers with the best, joining both sides of the watchpost image.
God declares that He takes vengeance upon criminals who turn from His signs, locating final redress in the divine claimant.
God takes vengeance on Pharaoh's people by drowning them for denying the signs, another direct case of the section's tyrant receiving divine requital.
The speaker commands that the prosperous deniers be left to Him and granted a little respite, the posture of a Lord personally holding their case until payment.
The reason for leaving the deniers to God is that shackles and a blazing fire are with Him, an unmatched penalty already held ready.
Choking food and painful punishment complete the prepared recompense announced in 73:11–12.
A questioner demands the punishment that will fall, repeating the section's motif of people impatiently summoning evil.
The demanded punishment belongs to the disbelievers and has no one able to repel it, giving divine requital the finality heard beside 89:25.
The unrepellable punishment comes from God, locating the claim above every human avenger.
The messenger is told not to hasten against the wrongdoers because God is counting out their term exactly, combining delay, surveillance, and certain reckoning.
At the arrival of punishment, the wrongdoers are reminded that they had sworn they would never pass away; 14:45 then places them among ruined predecessors and examples.
Moses says Pharaoh's people hold a blood charge against him and he fears they will kill him, a direct narrative of an unpaid killing generating threatened vengeance.
Moses says he killed one of Pharaoh's people and fears they will kill him, explicitly staging the reciprocal blood claim latent in the section's vetr imagery.
God recalls that Moses killed a person, was rescued from distress, and was tried through trials, compressing homicide and its feared aftermath into one divine account.
The command not to diminish people's goods expresses the human wrong of reducing another's due, against the assurance that God never diminishes earned deeds.
Full measure and weight are required and people's goods may not be diminished, another concrete form of withholding a right.
The people are forbidden to diminish others' goods and spread corruption, stating in social terms the deprivation named by the section's secondary w-t-r sense.
Woe is announced to those who give short measure, introducing a systematic human practice of diminishing others' rights that 83:2–3 specifies.
The defrauders demand full measure when receiving from others, showing the claimant's insistence on an undiminished due.
When measuring or weighing for others, the defrauders cause loss, the precise reversal of God's promise not to diminish works.
The defrauders are asked whether they expect to be resurrected, connecting hidden diminution of rights to the coming account.
No burdened soul can transfer any load even to a close relative, a family-specific bar against collective liability in a blood feud.

Those seeking only worldly life are paid their works there without diminution, but the following ayah denies them an afterlife share; it marks the boundary between immediate payment and lasting recompense.
The command not to kill a soul except by right repeats the legal boundary around bloodshed while placing it among duties to family and the vulnerable.
Believers are forbidden to kill one another, and 4:30 assigns fire to anyone who does so through aggression and injustice.
The unjust aggressor of 4:29 is promised the Fire, carrying communal homicide from human violation into divine punishment.
In a grave truth dispute, both parties are told to summon sons, women, and themselves and invoke God's curse on the liars; it is a family-involving oath ordeal that transfers judgment to God.
The deniers are asked whether they possess binding oaths from God lasting until Judgment that guarantee whatever they decide, exposing a false claim to control the final award.
A group of believers must witness the prescribed punishment, making the penalty publicly visible in the manner of an exemplary deterrent.
The record, prophets, and witnesses are brought and judgment is made in truth without injustice; 39:70 then states the full payment to every soul.
God sent messengers with proofs, took vengeance on the criminals, and declares support of believers His due, combining historical requital and preserved right.
The deniers ask to hasten God's punishment, repeating the impatience for evil before good named in the section.
When punishment descends into their courtyard, the warned people's morning will be terrible, answering 37:176's demand with the awaited event.
Those denying the signs are led gradually from where they do not know, describing a delayed requital that remains active while hidden.
God gives the deniers respite while His plan remains firm, the temporal counterpart of standing at a watchpost until the due time.
The respite given to disbelievers only lets them increase in sin before a humiliating punishment, so delay cannot be mistaken for a lost claim.
God tells the messenger to leave the deniers to Him while He draws them gradually from where they do not know, another image of personally reserved requital.
An evil deed receives a recompense like it, using the m-th-l root for exact equivalence rather than the exemplary punishment sense developed in the section.
Whoever brings good receives better, while evil-doers receive only the like of what they did; the m-th-l root again marks measured repayment with merciful asymmetry.
Pharaoh confronts Moses with the killing he committed, showing that the old blood charge remains remembered before Moses answers in 26:20–21.
Moses acknowledges committing the act while unaware of its course, supplying his own account of the killing invoked by Pharaoh.
Moses says he fled in fear after the killing and was later granted judgment and messengerhood, showing the blood claim's human danger and a different divine resolution.
A man exposes Moses by asking whether he means to kill him as he killed someone the previous day, making the concealed homicide publicly actionable.
A man warns Moses that the chiefs are plotting to kill him and urges flight, showing the retaliatory consequence of the killing reaching him.
God's seizure of wrongdoing towns is painful and severe, a general statement distilled from the exemplary destructions surrounding the section's named peoples.
The Lord's seizure is declared severe, reinforcing the claim that final divine punishment surpasses a human guardian's retaliation.
God takes vengeance on the two offending communities and leaves both sites visible on a clear road, making their punishment a standing warning.
